deep.reconstruction:
PROBLEM. The page solves the heat equation u_t = α² u_xx on the half-line x>0, with u=0 at t=0, under the radiation (Newton/Robin) boundary condition at x=0: ∂u/∂x − v u + a = 0, with a constant. Physically this is a semi-infinite rod with heat exchange at its end. The next page states the same condition as ∂u/∂x − νu + ω = 0 ('Lehrsatz I'). Gauss's notation Π(s)=Γ(s+1) is used throughout.

(1) DUHAMEL REPRESENTATION. u_τ(x,t) = ∫_{x/(2α√(t−τ))}^∞ e^{−y²} dy is the response to a unit step in boundary temperature switched on at time τ. Its boundary value is Π(½)=√π/2. Riemann superposes these:
u = ∫_0^t u_τ φ'(τ) dτ = ∫_0^t dτ ∫_{x/(2α√(t−τ))}^∞ φ'(τ) e^{−y²} dy.
Hence u(0,t) = Π(½)φ(t) [implicitly φ(0)=0].

(2) CHANGE OF ORDER. The region y > x/(2α√(t−τ)) is equivalent to (4α²/x²)(t−τ) > 1/y² > 0, i.e. t − x²/(4α²y²) > τ > 0, with y running from x/(2α√t) to ∞. So
u = ∫_{x/(2α√t)}^∞ e^{−y²} dy ∫_0^{t−x²/(4α²y²)} φ'(τ)dτ = ∫_{x/(2α√t)}^∞ e^{−y²} φ(t − x²/(4α²y²)) dy, using φ(0)=0.

(3) x-DERIVATIVE. The boundary term from the moving lower limit vanishes because φ(0)=0 [my remark]. Then
∂u/∂x = ∫ e^{−y²} φ'(t − x²/(4α²y²))·(−2x/(4α²y²)) dy.
With y = xz this becomes ∫_{1/(2α√t)}^∞ e^{−x²z²} φ'(t − 1/(4α²z²))·(−2dz/(4α²z²)).
With s = 1/(4α²z²) this becomes ∫_t^0 e^{−x²/(4α²s)} φ'(t−s)·(…)d(s^{−1/2}), hence
∂u/∂x = −(1/(2α)) ∫_0^t e^{−x²/(4α²s)} φ'(t−s) ds/√s.

(4) BOUNDARY EQUATION. At x=0 the condition becomes an Abel-type (half-derivative) integral equation for φ:
−(1/(2α)) ∫_0^t φ'(t−s) s^{−1/2} ds − v Π(½) φ(t) + a = 0, with abbreviation αv=β.
Substituting s = ty gives −(1/(2α)) ∫_0^1 φ'(t(1−y)) t dy/√(ty).

(5) POWER-SERIES ANSATZ. Take φ = Σ a_m t^m with m running over multiples of ½. Euler's Beta integral gives
∫_0^t m(t−s)^{m−1} s^{−1/2} ds = m t^{m−½} Π(m−1)Π(−½)/Π(m−½).
The equation becomes
−(1/(2α)) Σ a_m t^{m−½} m Π(m−1)Π(−½)/Π(m−½) − vΠ(½) Σ a_m t^m + a = 0.
Compare coefficients of t^m and divide by −Π(½), using Π(−½)/Π(½)=2 and mΠ(m−1)=Π(m) [my filling]:
(1/α) a_{m+½} Π(m+½)/Π(m) + v a_m = 0, i.e. b_{μ+1} = −αv b_μ where b_μ = a_{μ/2}Π(μ/2).
The constant term fixes a_{1/2} = 4αa/π.

(6) RIEMANN'S CLOSED-FORM ATTEMPT. He writes a_{(μ+1)/2} Π((μ+1)/2)/(αv)^{μ+1} = c, and so
φ(t) = Σ_{μ=1}^∞ c t^{μ/2} / (Π(μ/2)(−αv)^μ).
The correct recurrence gives (−αv)^{+μ} instead (see errors). With that correction,
φ = C Σ_{μ≥1} (−αv√t)^μ / Γ(μ/2+1) = C[e^{α²v²t} erfc(αv√t) − 1].

(7) DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION AND QUADRATURE. Riemann differentiates termwise:
φ' = c t^{−½}/(Π(−½)(−αv)) + c/(Π0·(−αv)²) + (remaining terms, which reproduce φ times a constant).
This gives a first-order linear ODE φ' − α²v²φ = (const) + (const)·t^{−½}. Multiplying by the integrating factor e^{−α²v²t} and integrating gives
e^{−α²v²t}φ(t) = ∫_0^t c' e^{−α²v²τ} dτ + ∫_0^t c'' e^{−α²v²τ} τ^{−½} dτ,
that is, an exponential plus an error-function integral.
The exponent α²v² is the correct one, which matches the corrected recurrence, not his written (αv)^{−μ}.
The final result [mine] is u(0,t) = Π(½)φ = (a/v)(1 − e^{α²v²t} erfc(αv√t)), the classical solution.

(8) OTHER MATERIAL. The upside-down German drafts are fragments of an expository text ('Wir werden … Bedeutung der … Functionen … Gebieten …'). They are probably related to the Abelian-functions/Riemann-surface material on the next page (Querschnitte, einfach zusammenhängend).
errors: Intermediate substitution line: the factor written as '−s^{1/2} ∂s^{−1/2}' cannot be right as transcribed. The correct factor is −(s/α) d(s^{−1/2}) = (1/(2α)) s^{−1/2} ds. The next line's result −(1/(2α))∫_0^t … ds/√s is nevertheless correct.
The recurrence (1/α)a_{m+½}Π(m+½)/Π(m) + v a_m = 0 gives a_{μ/2}Π(μ/2) ∝ (−αv)^{+μ}. Riemann writes a_{(μ+1)/2}Π((μ+1)/2)/(αv)^{μ+1} = c and φ = Σ c t^{μ/2}/(Π(μ/2)(−αv)^μ), with the power inverted.

The inverted power is also dimensionally inconsistent: αv has dimension T^{−1/2}, so the series must be in αv√t. His later integrating factor e^{−α²v²t} corresponds to the correct version, so this is a notational slip, not a conceptual error.

In the last line the left side is written as a t-derivative of e^{−α²v²t}φ while the right side is already integrated from 0 to t. The ∂ appears partly struck out; the intended statement is e^{−α²v²t}φ(t) = ∫_0^t (…)dτ.
The termwise derivative of the μ=2 term needs Π(0)=1, which he keeps symbolically. The tail φ/(αv)² relation is written and then struck out, consistent with his noticing the power problem.
Implicit but correct assumptions: φ(0)=0 (needed to drop boundary terms and for u(0,t)=Π(½)φ), and the legitimacy of exchanging the integrals.

results.what: Duhamel superposition of erfc step responses for the half-line heat equation, and reduction of the x-derivative at the boundary to −(1/(2α))∫_0^t φ'(t−s)s^{−1/2}ds
results.modern_name: Duhamel's principle; Dirichlet-to-Neumann map of the heat equation as a half-order time derivative
results.usually_credited_to: Duhamel (1833); half-derivative interpretation often associated with Heaviside (1890s) and later fractional-calculus literature

results.what: Robin/radiation boundary condition converted to an Abel-type integral equation and solved by a power series in √t via Euler's Beta integral
results.modern_name: Abel integral equation / fractional ODE D^{1/2}φ + λφ = f solved by a Mittag-Leffler series
results.usually_credited_to: Abel (1823), Liouville (1832); Riemann's own 1847 fractional-integration paper (published 1876); Mittag-Leffler function (1903)

results.what: Series Σ(−αv√t)^μ/Γ(μ/2+1) turned into the closed form e^{α²v²t}erfc(αv√t) via a first-order ODE with integrating factor
results.modern_name: Identity E_{1/2}(−z) = e^{z²}erfc(z); classical solution of semi-infinite solid with surface heat transfer
results.usually_credited_to: Classical heat-conduction theory (Fourier/Poisson era; standard form in Carslaw–Jaeger); Mittag-Leffler function 1903

deep.surprise_reason: The physical result (half-line heat conduction with radiation boundary condition) is classical, and Riemann's interest in heat conduction and fractional integration is well known. What is mildly notable is the method: reducing the boundary condition to a half-order Abel equation and solving it by a √t power series equivalent to the Mittag-Leffler function E_{1/2}, i.e. a Heaviside-style fractional-calculus treatment decades early. It is an unpublished private calculation containing an inversion slip, not a major new theorem.

Beta-integral step used for the power-series coefficients (expected 0)
Substitution s=1/(4α²z²) gives the kernel (1/(2α))s^{-1/2}ds, orientation reversed (expected 0)
Π(−½)/Π(½)=2, used to normalize the recurrence (expected 0)
Mittag-Leffler identity E_{1/2}(z)=e^{z²}erfc(−z), giving the closed form of the corrected series (expected ≈0)

transcription_corrections: The recurrence line is (1/α) a_{m+½} Π(m+½)/[Π m] + v a_m = 0. The denominator is blank in the transcription; Π(m) is required, and the faint image is consistent with it.
The margin note near the z-substitution, transcribed '2zα = √t', is more likely '2yα = √t' or a note on the limit y = x/(2α√t). Uncertain.
Intermediate line: '−s^{½} ∂s^{−½}' should probably read '−(s/α) ∂s^{−½}' or similar. The surviving image is unclear.
The last formula's left side 'd(e^{−α²v²t}φt)/dt' has the d/∂t partly struck in the image. The intended form is e^{−α²v²t}φ(t) = ∫_0^t … (an integrated identity).
Line '−(1/2α)∫_0^1 φ't(1−y) t dy/√(ty) [−√t−] + ½' should be read as −(1/(2α))∫_0^1 φ'(t(1−y)) t dy/√(ty). The crossed '√t' was rewritten as t^{½}.
